It is the measured behavioural effect of the summarizer — and the rig reproduces it exactly across repeats. So here is the sentence I would like people to take away: Replication is the preservation of causal behaviour , not of representation . An embedding cosine of 0.923 told us the text still looked like the payload. The metric that answers the propagation question said the payload was destroyed. If you measure memory poisoning with embedding similarity, you will get high numbers in exactly the case where the mechanism has stopped working. This is also why the retention levels are layered — exact, lexical, cosine, marker-token, functional — instead of collapsed into one "similarity" score. And why functional = null is honest rather than evasive: at write time, whether the payload survived cannot be decided. Only the action can decide it. Transferable practices If you run agents with memory, most of this is cheap to adopt: Log retrieval and context assembly as events, not inferences. Whether untrusted content reached the assembled prompt should be a field you can query, not something you reconstruct from vibes. Count parse failures and empty responses as first-class metrics. A model that never answered is not a model that resisted. Run the control that isolates persistence. The same prompt without the memory write tells you how much is prompt injection and how much is memory. Without that control you are measuring prompt injection and calling it a worm. Measure your noise floor before claiming an effect. Run the identical paired procedure on a carrier that does not exist. Treat retrieval k and score thresholds as experimental factors. "Propagation" is very easy to manufacture with a liberal top-k. Use a different model for every transformation. Summarizer, embedder, and agent sharing one model merges the memory effect with that model's idiosyncrasies. Pin model revisions by digest. An unpinned model revision makes the run unreproducible, full stop. Enforce trust at write time, not read time. Provenance, trust class, and TTL are first-class fields, because the write decision happens before state becomes durable. Checking at read time is trying to catch state that has already settled — a structurally weaker position. Concretely: an external source must not be able to write itself into a trusted class, and the rejection should be a logged event with a reason. Keep data and instruction separate, and keep agency least. A typed output schema constrains representation; a permission boundary constrains authority. Those are different controls, and you need both. What this does not show Being explicit about the envelope is part of the method, so: Δaction measures behavioural change, not harm. An inert canary that moves an agent does not mean a real payload would achieve anything in a production system with different policies, different retrieval, and a different capability ceiling. The rig answers "is persistence a working channel of influence," not "how dangerous is product X." The payloads are inert by construction. A trace id plus a request to call a stubbed tool that has no network and no filesystem access outside the run scratch directory. A payload policy screens every write and rejects operational content before it can become persistent. The model client is loopback-only and refuses non-loopback endpoints and configured external proxies. This is one machine, small local models, a synthetic world. Results generalize to architectural classes , not to specific products or to models at frontier scale. Known threats to validity , named in advance rather than after a convenient result: same model in several roles; liberal retrieval masquerading as propagation; model stochasticity read as adaptation; an agent that "senses" a test harness; the lab-versus-reality gap; and selective reporting — hypotheses get pre-registered, and runs that show nothing stay in the report. One honest caveat on the headline finding: the summarizer destroyed the trace id but kept a different identifier (the marker token) and the instruction text. Whether an agent would act on that remainder is an open question, because the rig currently only treats the trace id as the payload's identity. That gap is the next roadmap item, not a footnote I get to hide — the fix is to give each payload several independent identifiers so that "the payload survived" and "an identifier survived" become two separate, testable statements. The rig is private and unlicensed at the moment, so there is no clone-and-run link in this post — which is why the key mechanisms are inlined above rather than gestured at. What is measurable is reproducible: 125 stdlib-only tests, deterministic scripted control runs, and pinned model digests. Where the framing comes from The conceptual framing here — treating a propagating payload as something to be typed and measured rather than asserted, and separating evidence , inference , and speculation — follows the AI-virology write-ups published at vxheaven.ru , in particular their analysis of the Morris II self-replicating-prompt experiments ( Cohen, Bitton & Nassi, Here Comes The AI Worm: Unleashing Zero-click Worms that Target GenAI-Powered Applications , arXiv:2403.02817 , v2, January 2025). Note what that paper is and is not: it demonstrated a chain reaction of indirect prompt injection across RAG-based email assistants in a controlled ecosystem, and evaluated a guardrail (Virtual Donkey) reporting a 1.0 true-positive rate at a 0.015 false-positive rate. It is a proof of concept about architectural connectivity — not evidence of a universal Internet worm. The authors' own ethical considerations state that all experiments were run in a lab precisely to avoid releasing a worm into the wild, and that they did not test the guardrail against adaptive attacks. That distinction is the same one this post is making about zeros: the claim has to match what was actually measured. Further reading If you want the standards-track version of practices 8 and 9 above, rather than one person's rig: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 — prompt injection as a root-cause risk, plus vector/embedding and excessive-agency entries. OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026 — agent behaviour hijacking, tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse. NIST AI 100-2 E2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations — useful for naming attacks precisely instead of borrowing "worm" for anything that propagates text. Anthropic, Mitigating the risk of prompt injections in browser use — a vendor stating plainly that prompt injection is not solved, with measured residual risk. OpenAI, Designing AI agents to resist prompt injection — treats serious real-world injection as closer to social engineering than to a prompt override. The measurements in this post are my own, from the local rig described above. Any errors in them are mine, and if you reproduce them and get different numbers, the reproduction wins. If you build agents with persistent memory, the cheapest useful thing you can do this week is (2) and (4): count the responses that never answered, and measure what your rig does when there was nothing there to measure.

title: I Built Interactive CLI Drills — Learners Quit at Prompt #3
author: arnostorg
summary: I Built Interactive CLI Drills — Learners Quit at Prompt #3 I built what I wanted as a learner: interactive CLI drills in the browser. Type commands. Get feedback. No “install fifteen tools first.” Then the analytics (and the hallway conversations) said something rude: a chunk of learners quit at prompt #3. This is a show-and-tell about that product bruise—and what I changed. What I shipped first Short missions for CMD, PowerShell, and Bash-oriented tasks on Windows-friendly paths. Immediate correctness checks. A clean terminal UI that feels like practice, not a MOOC video. The thesis: skill is built at the prompt. Screenshots weren’t enough (I had already burned myself on that experiment). Prompt #3: the cliff Patterns in the drop-off: Prompt #1 was a win (list files, print a string). Dopamine. Prompt #2 introduced one new concept. Still okay. Prompt #3 combined concepts—or required recovery from error—without a scaffold. Confidence cratered. It wasn’t “students are lazy.” It was difficulty curve arrogance. I had optimized for correctness of the skill model, not for the emotional runway of a first session. Product fixes that mattered Smaller concept steps One idea per prompt until the streak feels earned. Combine later in a “mission boss,” not at step three. Intentional recovery prompts Instead of only happy paths, add a safe failure that teaches ERRORLEVEL / $LASTEXITCODE early— after a success, not instead of one. Shell labeling everywhere Ambiguity across CMD vs PowerShell was silent quit fuel. Labels and prompts now scream which contract you’re in. Softer first-session definition of done A complete first session can be six tiny wins. Heroics can be session two. What I’d still defend Interactive > passive for CLI. The quit data didn’t kill the thesis; it killed my pacing ego. Also: soft CTAs beat launch-speak. The product exists to train operators, not to win a landing-page award. Where it lives Instrumentation that changed my mind I stopped celebrating completion rate alone. I started watching: median time-to-first-success, drop-off by prompt index, repeat visits within 48 hours, qualitative “I felt dumb” comments (painful, gold). Prompt #3 was the cliff on the first curriculum graph. After re-pacing, the cliff moved later—and got shorter. That’s product work, not vibes. What “showdev” means here Not a launch. A build diary: interactive Windows CLI practice is the medium; curriculum pacing is the hard problem; soft CTA is intentional. If you’re building a trainer, steal the quit-index chart idea before you polish marketing copy. Design smell: “clever” early combines If prompt #3 needs two new ideas and perfect quoting and an error recovery, you didn’t write a drill—you wrote a hazing ritual. Split it. Clever can wait until the streak feels real. What I almost did wrong next I almost responded to quit data by adding badges and streaks—gamification as a bandage. Maybe later. First fix was honesty about pacing. If the third prompt is a cliff, glitter won’t pave it. Make the third prompt a fair win, then earn the harder combines. The drills are free and browser-based: CMD Master —interactive terminal learning for CMD, PowerShell, and Bash. If you try it, watch where you want to bail. That spot is probably my next design ticket. Open build question For those who’ve built coding or ops trainers: do you gate progress strictly, or let learners skip and return? I’m still torn between “force the reps” and “don’t imprison adults.” Show-and-tell, not victory lap: prompt #3 humbled the roadmap.

title: A shared media gallery for chats and profiles
author: Frank Milvus
summary: Open a friend's profile — or a group's info screen — and you can now browse every photo, video, document and link the two participants have exchanged. We call it the shared media gallery , a familiar idea from other messengers, scoped tightly to the conversation between you. The important word there is conversation-scoped . The gallery is not a cross-chat index of everything a user ever sent; it's the media belonging to one thread. On a profile that thread is the 1:1 chat between you and the person; in group info it's the group. One read serves both shapes, and the profile reaches it through a read-only peer resolver that never creates a conversation as a side effect. It shipped as Phase 1, and this post walks through the parts that were worth getting right: the single conversation-scoped read, its kind slices, cursor pagination, the resolver, a small FastAPI routing gotcha, and why encrypted chats are deliberately left out. Why scope the gallery to a conversation The obvious alternative is a user-scoped media index: "everything this person has ever shared, across all their chats." We didn't want that, for two reasons. First, the feature's meaning is always conversational. When you open someone's profile and tap Media , you're asking "what have the two of us shared?" When you open group info, you're asking "what has this group shared?" Both questions are about a single conversation, and answering them with a per-user index would force us to reconstruct the conversation boundary in the query anyway. Second, access control falls out for free. A conversation already has a membership check on every read, so the gallery inherits it: if you're not a member, you can't page through the media. No new sharing model, no new leak surface. So the primitive is simple: given a conversation and a caller, return the messages in that conversation that carry media. One read serves 1:1 and groups The backend exposes a single service method, fetch_shared_media , and both entry points delegate to it: @staticmethod async def fetch_shared_media ( db : AsyncSession , conversation_id : int , user_id : int , kind : str = " media " , limit : int = 50 , before : int | None = None , ): """ Messages carrying media in a conversation (the " Shared Media " gallery shown on a profile and in group info). """ It verifies the caller's access to the conversation, refuses encrypted threads (more on that below), filters by kind, and returns newest-first. The same call powers a 1:1 profile tab and a group screen; there is no "group variant" and no "profile variant" on the read path. The kind slices A gallery isn't one list — it's three, and the frontend shows them as segments. The kind argument selects the slice: image — messages with an image attached. video — messages with a video attached. media (the default) — images and videos, which is the photos grid. file — documents, i.e. messages carrying a file attachment. link — messages the backend attached a link preview to. The filters are plain column checks, which keeps the slice logic in one place and easy to read: if kind == " image " : kind_filter = Message . image_url . is_not ( None ) elif kind == " video " : kind_filter = Message . video_url . is_not ( None ) elif kind == " file " : kind_filter = Message . file_url . is_not ( None ) elif kind == " link " : kind_filter = Message . link_preview_url . is_not ( None ) else : # "media" (default): images and videos kind_filter = or_ ( Message . image_url . is_not ( None ), Message . video_url . is_not ( None ), ) link is worth a note: it doesn't mean "message text contains a URL." It means the backend unfurled the URL and stored a preview, which is exactly what the link list renders. Deleted messages, ordering, and the cursor Two invariants keep the list honest. Deleted messages are excluded outright — deleted_at IS NULL is part of the WHERE , so a removed photo doesn't linger in the grid. And results are ordered Message.id.desc() , newest first, matching how every other list in the app reads. Pagination is a keyset cursor, not an offset: pass before , the id of the oldest message you've already seen, and the query adds Message.id < before . That stays correct while new messages arrive — an offset would shift rows out from under the reader as the conversation grows. The route takes the same three knobs, so the client can fetch the first page and then ask for older media on demand. There's one subtle, very real backend detail here. The response serializes the reply sender's name, so reply_to.sender is eager-loaded on the query. A lazy load inside an async session raises MissingGreenlet at serialization time — the same bug family we hit on search. It's the kind of thing that only shows up when a gallery item happens to be a reply to an image, which makes it exactly the kind of thing to pin down in a query rather than discover in production. A read-only peer resolver that never creates a conversation The profile screen knows a user id, not a conversation id. Normally "start a chat" means get-or-create: look for the conversation, and if it isn't there, make one. That's the wrong contract for a profile tab. Opening someone's profile is a read , and it shouldn't quietly create an empty conversation just because they glanced at a Media tab. So the peer path is a dedicated resolver, fetch_shared_media_with_user , and it resolves without ever writing: low , high = ( user_id , peer_id ) if user_id <= peer_id else ( peer_id , user_id ) stmt = ( select ( Conversation . id ) . where ( Conversation . type == " private " , Conversation . is_encrypted . is_ ( False ), Conversation . user_low == low , Conversation . user_high == high , ) . order_by ( Conversation . id . asc ()) . limit ( 1 ) ) conversation_id = ( await db . execute ( stmt )). scalars (). first () if conversation_id is None : return [] return await ChatService . fetch_shared_media ( db , conversation_id , user_id , ...) The pair is normalized to an ordered (low, high) so both directions of the same 1:1 point at one row. The lookup is restricted to a plaintext private conversation and returns an empty list when there isn't one — never a new row. From there it delegates to the same fetch_shared_media , so the resolver only ever has to know how to find a conversation, not how to read its media. That "returns empty when none exists" behaviour is what makes the read idempotent: call it once or a hundred times, the state of the database is identical. Two routes, and the literal-first ordering gotcha The API exposes two endpoints: GET /chat/with/{user_id}/media?kind=&limit=&before= GET /chat/{conversation_id}/media?kind=&limit=&before= The first is for profiles (peer id), the second for groups and chat info (conversation id). Both map onto the service methods above. Here's the gotcha, and it's a genuine one. The second route's path segment is {conversation_id} , a placeholder that will happily match any single segment — including the literal string with . If it were declared first, a request to /chat/with/123/media would match that placeholder, FastAPI would then try to validate with as an integer, and the client would get a 422 rather than the profile gallery. FastAPI resolves routes in declaration order and validates the path parameter's type after a route matches, so a later literal route is simply never reached. The rule that follows is boring and effective: declare the literal, more-specific route first. We do, and the with segment can never be mistaken for a conversation id. The FastAPI docs on path parameters and their order are worth a read if you haven't been bitten by this yet. Encrypted chats are deliberately excluded We ship opt-in end-to-end encrypted chats. Their media is encrypted on the client before it ever reaches the server, which means the server is holding ciphertext — and ciphertext can't be filtered or listed. There is no "is this an image?" column to query, because the image is inside a blob the server can't read. So the feature is honest about it in two different places: The conversation-scoped read checks whether the conversation is encrypted and returns 403 if it is — "Shared media is not available in encrypted chats." An explicit refusal beats a silently empty list that looks like a bug. The peer resolver only ever looks at the plaintext private conversation, so a profile Media tab for someone you only share an encrypted chat with simply returns nothing. It doesn't 403, because from the resolver's point of view the two of you have no plaintext conversation — which is true. Making this work later means decrypting from the local cache on the client, a separate effort we've noted rather than bolted on. Some things are worth doing once, properly. The frontend: Media / Files / Links The Flutter side is a single reusable widget, SharedMediaView . It takes exactly one of userId (profile path) or conversationId (group path), asserted at construction, and stores three lazy segment caches so switching tabs doesn't re-fetch what you've already seen. The segments are Media, Files and Links, switched with Material's SegmentedButton , and the Media segment renders a 3-up grid that reuses the pieces the rest of the app already has: CachedNetworkImage backed by the shared AppMediaCacheManager for cached thumbnails, and the existing fullscreen gallery for the tap-through, so the gallery you get here behaves exactly like the one in a chat. Videos render a play-button placeholder in the grid and open in the same viewer. Files and links are lists. A file row shows the file name and a human-readable size and opens in the browser on tap. A link row leads with the unfurled thumbnail, then the preview title, with the site name underneath — the same data the link-preview message bubble uses, which is why the link slice keys off the stored preview rather than parsing text. For entry points that aren't already a tab — pushing the gallery from group info — a thin SharedMediaScreen hosts the widget full-screen. The profile reuses its tab framework, adding an optional Media tab scoped by userId . If you like the media plumbing behind this, two sibling posts go deeper: photo albums in Flutter covers the multi-image layout, and the Flutter Linux desktop video and media kit covers playback. The session durability work with the Linux keyring is the other half of getting desktop right, and there's a full overview of tonGues if you're new here. FAQ Does opening someone's profile create a chat? No. The profile path goes through the read-only peer resolver, which returns an empty list when the two of you have no plaintext conversation. It never writes a row. What happens on an encrypted chat? The conversation-scoped endpoint returns 403 — an explicit "not available here." The profile path returns an empty list, because the resolver only consults the plaintext 1:1 conversation. Can the gallery show media from a group and a 1:1 the same way? Yes. Both are the same conversation-scoped read; the only difference is whether the client passes a conversationId or resolves one from a userId . Do deleted messages still show up? No. Deleted messages are excluded at the query level, so a removed photo disappears from the grid on the next load. Can I page further back through old media? The API is cursor-paginated by message id via before , newest-first. The Phase 1 UI loads the first page; wiring the grid's scroll to pull older pages is a small follow-up on the same cursor. — the tonGues team Get tonGues — a language-exchange messenger with live translation. title: Taming Local Disk Bloat: Where Did My 512GB Mac SSD Go and How to Clean It Safely
author: Sarmad Hussain
summary: Every developer working on a Mac has encountered that sudden, dreaded system alert: ⚠️ "Your disk is almost full" You open System Settings → General → Storage , hoping for answers. Instead, macOS gives you a massive, mysterious gray bar labeled: System Data: 142 GB What on earth is in that 142 GB? Why is it growing? And more importantly: how do you reclaim it without corrupting your active Git repositories or breaking your dev environment? In this guide, we'll dissect the real culprits behind hidden developer disk bloat on macOS, provide native Terminal commands to find them, and explain how to clean them safely. 1. The Real Culprits Behind Developer Disk Bloat Standard Mac cleaners scan for browser cookies, language packs, and user caches. But for developers, those are trivial pennies. The real gigabyte-scale storage hogs are buried in your developer toolchains: Storage Hog Typical Size Where It Hides Orphaned node_modules 20 GB – 80 GB Forgotten tutorial projects, abandoned feature branches Xcode DerivedData & Simulators 30 GB – 70 GB ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData Docker VM Overlays & BuildKit 25 GB – 60 GB ~/Library/Containers/com.docker.docker/Data/vms Gradle & Maven Caches 10 GB – 30 GB ~/.gradle/caches , ~/.m2/repository Homebrew Downloads & Stale Bottles 5 GB – 15 GB ~/Library/Caches/Homebrew WhatsApp / Slack Desktop Media 15 GB – 40 GB ~/Library/Group Containers/group.net.whatsapp.WhatsApp.shared 2. Terminal Deep-Dive: Finding Bloat with Native Commands Before running third-party scripts, let's inspect our disk using native Unix utilities already built into macOS. Finding Forgotten node_modules Directories If you've been developing in JavaScript, TypeScript, or React for a couple of years, you likely have dozens of stale projects lingering in your ~/Projects , ~/Sites , or ~/Developer folders. To find all node_modules folders taking up more than 500MB: find ~/Projects -name "node_modules" -type d -prune -exec du -sh {} + 2>/dev/null | sort -hr | head -n 20 Warning: Never delete node_modules blindly using global rm -rf scripts while an active project is compiling or using symbolic links. Finding Xcode DerivedData Bloat Every time you compile an iOS or macOS app in Xcode, index files, intermediate build objects, and module caches accumulate: du -sh ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData 2>/dev/null If that folder is over 30 GB, you can safely wipe its contents: rm -rf ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/ * (Xcode will seamlessly regenerate whatever it needs during your next build). Inspecting Docker Storage Docker on macOS runs inside a lightweight Linux virtual machine disk image ( Docker.raw or Docker.qcow2 ). Over time, unreferenced images, stopped containers, and build cache layers expand this virtual disk to maximum capacity: docker system df To safely reclaim unused Docker build cache and dangling images: docker system prune --volumes 3. The Trust Problem: Why Traditional Cleaners Fail Developers Traditional "one-click" Mac cleaning software operates like an opaque black box: They report a vague counter: "24.8 GB of System Junk found!" They ask for full disk access permissions. They delete files with zero explanation of what they actually were. And worse: they demand $40/year recurring subscriptions for a basic cron job. When a cleaner touches a developer's machine, trust is paramount. Deleting a configuration file in ~/Library/Application Support or removing a SQLite database from a local test environment can cost hours of debugging. 4. Introducing Dusty: AI-Explained macOS Storage Management To solve this trust gap, we built Dusty natively in Swift and SwiftUI. Dusty is engineered specifically for developers and power users who need complete transparency and surgical control over their disk space. Key Architectural Pillars: Plain-English AI Explanations: When inspecting obscure cache files in ~/Library/Caches , Dusty connects to Google Gemini AI to analyze file headers and directory trees. It explains in plain English: What application created this file? Why is it taking up this much space? Is it safe to delete, or will it cause an app to re-index? Developer Bloat Scanner: Directly targets node_modules , Xcode DerivedData , Docker container overlays, Gradle caches, and .next build caches across all project directories. Surgical WhatsApp Media Cleaner: Scans WhatsApp Desktop storage and lets you safely reclaim gigabytes of forwarded videos and audio notes without touching your chat history or ChatStorage.sqlite . Trash-First Safety Architecture: Nothing is permanently deleted without your explicit review. Every cleaned file moves safely to native macOS Trash first, so you can inspect or restore it at any time. Zero Subscriptions: An honest $9.99 lifetime license (with a 24-hour full free trial). Pay once, own forever. 5. Quick Install via Homebrew You can install Dusty in seconds directly through Homebrew: brew install sarmadhussainch/dusty/dusty Or download the universal binary (Apple Silicon M1/M2/M3/M4 & Intel) directly from the official website: 🔗 https://dustystorage.com GitHub Tap: https://github.com/sarmadhussainch/homebrew-dusty Summary Checklist for Developer Disk Hygiene Run find or use an analyzer to audit old node_modules directories. Flush ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData every few months. Run docker system prune when disk space dips below 20%. Clean WhatsApp Desktop forwarded media attachments. Keep your Mac SSD at least 15% free so APFS wear-leveling and swap memory perform optimally! What's the biggest storage hog you've discovered on your Mac? Let me know in the comments below!

title: Red Once: never trust a test you haven't watched fail
author: Chuks Adirije
summary: My visual regression check reported zero pixels changed across 28 screenshots. Every one of those pages had a bright red background injected into it. 28 screenshots compared 0 px changed PASS Three separate defects were queuing up behind that zero. The check had been green since the day it was written, which is exactly what made it worthless. The thing that changed Test-driven development asks you to write a failing test before the code. Most engineers have never worked that way, and the profession has largely made peace with that. Tests get written after, or alongside, the suite goes green, and life continues. That peace held because writing a test by hand carried some verification as a side effect. You had to imagine the failure in order to type the assertion. You pictured the thing breaking, decided what breaking looked like, and wrote that down. Nobody called it a methodology, but it was doing real work. An agent generating forty tests from an implementation that already passes does none of that. It reads what the code does and asserts that the code does it. Every assertion is true at the moment it is written, by construction, and none of them has ever distinguished a working system from a broken one. The output is a suite that raises coverage while verifying nothing. It is harder to catch than a missing test, because it looks reviewed. Agents produce well-named, well-shaped, arrange-act-assert tests. They look like the work of someone careful. What the red step was actually for The ordering in TDD exists to deliver one guarantee: that a human being has personally watched this assertion distinguish broken from working. Writing the test first is simply the most convenient moment to collect that guarantee, because the code does not exist yet and red is free. Which means the guarantee is separable from the ordering. You can write the code first, the way nearly everyone and every agent actually works, and still collect it. You just have to pay for it afterwards, deliberately, instead of getting it for free. The pattern: Red Once No assertion is trusted until you have watched it fail, for the reason you think it fails. Performed at the moment a test is authored, not retroactively across an existing suite. 1. Break the code under test One change, inside the code under test. Invert a condition. Return a constant. Delete the line that does the work. Rename the column the query selects. Editing the test instead proves nothing, because a test can always be made to fail by breaking the test. 2. Run that one test and read the failure It has to go red, and the message has to name the thing you broke. $ pytest tests/test_balance.py::test_excludes_body_only -x FAILED assert 4200 == 3900 where 4200 = invoice_total(session) 1 failed in 0.41s 3. Restore, re-run, and write down what you broke Green again, and the mutation recorded next to the test. One line is enough. def test_excludes_body_only ( session ): # red-once: returned the unfiltered total from # invoice_total() -> 4200 != 3900. 2026-10-13. assert invoice_total ( session ) == 3900 This is the step everybody skips, and it is the one that turns a private act of diligence into something the next person can repeat. Where it sits Red for the right reason A test that fails is not automatically a test that works. It can go red because an import blew up, a fixture collapsed, a migration had not run, a network call timed out, or a mock went stale. All of those produce red, and none of them tells you anything about your assertion. So step 2 has two conditions, and the second one is the real one: it failed, and the failure names the thing you broke. If you inverted a filter and the test reports a connection error, you have learned nothing and you are not finished. This is the same error that produced the red page and the zero. The check passed for a reason that had nothing to do with the pages matching: the diff library painted unchanged pixels as faded grey, the test read colour channels for any value at all, so nearly every pixel registered as unstable and the mask built to ignore instability grew to cover the entire page. A correct answer arrived by a route that could never have produced a wrong one. What was hiding behind the zero The harness was wrong three ways at once, and all three were invisible to a green run. The mask ate the page. The diff library paints unchanged pixels as faded greyscale rather than leaving them transparent. The comparison tested colour channels for any value, so almost every pixel counted as changed, and the instability mask covered everything. Reading the alpha channel instead fixed it. A footer that was never photographed. Screenshots captured the viewport. One of the footers sat four thousand pixels down the page. Two sides on different frames. The CSS animations were keyed to page load, so the comparison was never made at the same moment in the animation, and the drift was absorbed as noise. There was a fourth problem in the threshold itself. It was expressed as a ratio of total pixels, which scales with page height, so the longer the page the more a real regression could hide inside an acceptable percentage. Absolute pixel counts, set just above a measured noise floor, do not have that property. All four surfaced within an hour of injecting a regression the check was supposed to catch and refusing to accept green. Make the agent do it This is the part that makes the discipline survive contact with how software is now written. An agent that can write a test can also break the code, run the test, and show you the failure. It is a strictly mechanical sequence, which is the kind of work agents are good at. Add it to your agent instructions, and require the evidence rather than the assurance: After writing a test, prove it discriminates: 1. make one change to the code under test that should break it 2. run that test alone, capture the output 3. confirm the failure names what you changed 4. revert, re-run, confirm green Paste both outputs. Do not describe them. The captured failure is the artifact. It goes in the pull request next to the diff, and it changes what a reviewer is looking at. A recorded failure is a receipt, and a reviewer can check it in seconds. The old review question The question that survives agents Is there a test for this? Has this test ever failed? Answerable by looking. Satisfied by anything shaped like a test. Answerable only with evidence, and the evidence is cheap to produce and impossible to fake by accident. What it costs, and where it stops About a minute per test. Break, run one test, read, revert, note. One case, start to finish. It is not retroactive. Nobody is going to go back through four thousand existing tests. Do it at authoring time, and do it for any test standing guard over something whose failure would be expensive or silent. One mutant is enough. The goal is to establish that the assertion discriminates at all, not to prove it catches every possible defect. It does not replace the tools. Mutation testing frameworks do this exhaustively and automatically. If you can run one, run it. On the name and the idea None of the mechanism here is new. Deliberately breaking code to confirm a test notices is the manual form of mutation testing, which has been studied since the 1970s and has mature tooling: Stryker , PIT , mutmut . What changed is the cost of skipping it. For decades this was a nicety, because hand-writing a test did some of the work incidentally. Generated tests do none of that work, so the step everyone used to skip is now the one holding the suite up. It needed a short name and a place in the workflow. Write the code first if you want, but never trust an assertion you have not watched fail for the right reason. That is all of Red Once .

title: The Boredom Premium: How DeFi Stopped Being a Casino
author: Woof
summary: Less than 1% of DeFi's TVL carries insurance, versus 80-95% in TradFi, because opt-in coverage models trigger an "adverse selection death spiral" that has killed every prior DeFi insurer. Catalysis, built with Woof Software's Mykola Ilchuk, fixes this by making coverage vault-native and default — not optional to unlock institutional capital. Amsterdam, 1774: The “Pre-seed” of the modern world. A merchant named Abraham van Ketwich did something the Amsterdam exchange had never seen before - he made investing boring. His creation, Eendragt Maakt Magt (“Unity Creates Strength”), became the world’s first modern investment fund. It didn't promise spectacular returns. It promised diversification, a modest yield, and, most importantly, the ability to sleep through the night without worrying about your money. The Dutch aristocracy loved it, not because it was exciting, but precisely because it wasn't. 250 years later, this “boring” idea manages $6.3 trillion in American money market funds alone. Nobody checks their money market balance every morning. Nobody joins a Discord to discuss “to the moon” strategies for Treasury bills. The money just sits there, it grows, and you forget about it. This condition - where financial infrastructure becomes so reliable that the user simply forgets it exists - is the Boredom Premium. And it is likely the largest market opportunity that DeFi has yet to capture. The Pattern Nobody Talks About Every financial technology in human history has passed through the same five stages of the market cycle. No exceptions. 1920s, “Bucket Shops”: For the first time, ordinary Americans rushed to trade stocks, not realizing their “exchanges” never actually placed their orders on any market. The 1929 crash forced the creation of the SEC, FDIC, and federal deposit insurance. This was boring regulation that made banking safe for the masses. 1980s, “Junk Bonds”: Michael Milken (an American financier known as the "junk bond king" for his role in developing the market for high-yield bonds) argued that the market was underpricing yield. After a decade of euphoria, Drexel Burnham Lambert - the powerhouse Wall Street investment bank that fueled this entire junk bond craze - collapsed into bankruptcy. The result: rating agencies gained real enforcement power. Boring, but the system survived. 2000s, MBS (Mortgage-Backed Securities): The legend that “housing prices never go down”. Turns out, they do. The response: Dodd-Frank (2010 comprehensive Wall Street reform law that heavily increased regulation, stress-testing, and consumer protections) and TARP (2008 government bailout that bought toxic MBS and injected capital into banks). This kicked off the most tedious era in banking history. Banks are still paying for this boredom, and that’s exactly why they remain solvent today. 2020s, DeFi Summer: “Number go up”. Then Luna. Then FTX. Then Euler. The response: a graveyard of first-generation insurance protocols that collapsed under the weight of their own flawed tokenomics, and a wave of undercollateralized credit platforms (think Celsius or BlockFi) that blew up the moment real market stress tested their spreadsheets. The pattern is immutable: Excitement → Crisis → Infrastructure → Boredom → Scale. DeFi is currently stuck between Crisis and Infrastructure. The question isn't whether DeFi will become boring, it's who builds the rails for that boredom. Infographic chart illustrating the 5-stage financial technology cycle from bucket shops to modern DeFi scalability. Cultural Code and the “Adverse Selection Death Spiral” Why does nobody insure the thing they worry about most? We insure our cars, our houses, our teeth, and even our fantasy football teams. But we don't insure our capital in DeFi - the thing we worry about most. Less than 1% of DeFi TVL carries any form of coverage, while in TradFi, that figure is 80–95%. Billions of dollars sit in smart contracts without a single “parachute”. Not for lack of tools, but because nobody is buying them. The reasons are brutally simple: It's painfully expensive (often eating 50-80% of your net yield). The UX is fragmented (forcing users to hunt down coverage on secondary protocols). The payouts are subjective (relying on opaque DAO governance votes rather than deterministic code). But beneath these friction points lies a deeper, structural flaw where psychology and poor market design violently collide. This is where it gets interesting. Psychology and poor market design collide here. Historically, DeFi culture was built on an unwritten, binary code: you’re either completely bullish, or you shouldn't be here. For years, actively seeking downside protection was viewed by the crypto-native crowd almost as an admission of weakness - like showing up to a party and loudly announcing you think the roof might cave in. But while retail degens might enjoy playing financial roulette, institutional capital does not. The fact that 95–98% of DeFi capital remains uncovered isn't just a quirk of crypto psychology anymore; it's a symptom of a market that forces users to actively opt-in to their own anxiety. And mathematically, this opt-in model triggers a fatal economic chain reaction. It has a name: the Adverse Selection Death Spiral, which has killed every previous attempt to create DeFi insurance until today. The mechanics of this collapse are mathematically inevitable: You launch a protocol where coverage is strictly opt-in. Who buys first? The highest-risk actors sitting in the most vulnerable pools-the ones actively expecting an exploit. The risk pool becomes hyper-concentrated with toxic exposure. Claim frequency rises, forcing premiums to skyrocket. Conservative capital in safe vaults looks at the 5%+ premium, realizes it destroys their net yield, and walks away. Premiums climb even higher to compensate. Only the most desperate remain. The system collapses. This isn't a theoretical model; it’s the literal post-mortem of the first-generation DeFi insurance market. Look at Nexus Mutual: $200M in reserves trapped behind 36-to-72-hour manual claims, subjective governance votes on payouts, and opaque underwriting. Look at what happened to InsurAce, Ease (Armor.fi), Unslashed, and Neptune Mutual. When the 2022 stress tests hit (the UST depeg and FTX collapse), on-chain insurers faced roughly $34M in claims - about 90% of all historical payouts - instantly overwhelming their liquid capacity. Unslashed had written $400 million in coverage against a mere $90 million in capital. The B3i consortium, backed by 20+ global TradFi reinsurers, burned through $23M and went bankrupt without ever solving the core inefficiency. Previous DeFi insurance wasn't killed by bad code. It was killed by a critical error in market design. Circular architecture diagram showing the mechanics of the adverse selection insurance death spiral in early DeFi.rance Death Spiral The Catalysis Play: Coverage as a Default Layer Now imagine a different scenario. Coverage is embedded directly into the vault. By default. You deposit - you’re covered. Period. In this model, adverse selection is flipped on its head. We aren't gathering paranoiacs into a single pool; we’re covering everyone. Retail and institutions, the cautious and the carefree. Risk is distributed across a broad base instead of concentrating among the anxious few. The result: premiums drop, underwriter revenue stabilizes, and users don't have to "admit they're nervous" - the coverage is simply there. We call these Catalysis Covered Vaults: pools where downside protection is not a feature you buy, but a property of the vault itself. Nobody “buys” FDIC insurance. You open a bank account, and your first $250,000 is covered. It’s not a feature of the bank; it’s a feature of the system. Comparative illustration of Alice in 2023 vs 2026 highlighting default vault-native coverage in Catalysis. Engineering the Boredom: The Invisible Infrastructure Catalysis builds vault-native coverage that actually works because it removes human hesitation from the loop. Risk is isolated. Payouts are deterministic. No governance committees are debating your claim for three weeks - just code executing, slashing when predefined conditions are met. If you want the deep dive into the exact architecture, how restaked capital secures the pools, and the math behind contagion-free CoverPools, we broke down the entire technical stack here: https://x.com/0xcatalysis/status/2021236666925494321?s=20 . What actually matters right now is what this looks like for the end user. And realistically, it looks like nothing. There are no extra buttons to click, no premiums to manually calculate, and no secondary protocols to visit. You simply deposit your capital, and the downside is capped by default. For the user, the anxiety of DeFi is entirely abstracted away. By making the complex risk-management machinery completely invisible, Catalysis isn't just launching another DeFi product. It is building the exact baseline infrastructure required to absorb the next massive wave of institutional liquidity. The Trillion-Dollar Standard: Scaling New Financial Rails In 2020, DeFi was a $13 billion market. Projections put it at $1.4 trillion by the early 2030s. But those trillions won't come from flashy APYs chased by crypto-native degens. They will come from corporate treasurers, pension funds, and family offices - people whose entire job is finding safe, boring yield. According to the Coinbase-EY 2026 Institutional Investor Survey, 43% of institutions plan to engage with DeFi protocols within the next two years, on top of the 13% already using them - and they aren't waiting for more exciting features. Their top three concerns tell the whole story: security (85%), regulatory uncertainty (84%), and compliance (81%). They're waiting for downside protection.The future of DeFi is about you not knowing that you’re using DeFi. In ten years, your money will sit in a DeFi vault, and you won't know it’s DeFi, and you won't care. That will be the ultimate win. The signals are already here. Coinbase Earn now routes USDC through curated Morpho vaults. Kraken's DeFi Earn, launched in early 2026 with Veda infrastructure and Chaos Labs risk management, pipes retail deposits into Aave and Morpho without users ever touching a wallet. The pattern is consistent: users want yield, but they want it risk-adjusted - whether they're retail or institutional. This isn't new behavior. TradFi users have always accepted lower yield in exchange for downside protection. DeFi simply hasn't offered that natively and efficiently - until now. Covered vaults unlock that latent demand. Catalysis is building the infrastructure that makes that boredom possible. By Mykola Ulchuk - R&D Technical Researcher at Woof and Abishek Kumar - Founder & CEO at Catalysis Contact @woof_software today!

title: Build a Chatbot in Python From Scratch: No API Keys, No AI Libraries
author: RainyTech
summary: Most "build a chatbot" tutorials are really "call someone else's API" tutorials. This one isn't. We build Nova , a small chatbot that learns from examples, using only Python's standard library for the AI part, plus FastAPI to serve it to a web chat page. No API key, no paid service, no model download. Every line of the classifier fits on one screen. Full source code: https://github.com/rainyreaksmey/build-chatbot-from-scratch Every number in this post comes from running that repo. Nova is an intent chatbot, not a large language model. It doesn't write new sentences. It recognizes what you mean and picks a matching answer. That's exactly how many real FAQ and support bots work. 1. How an intent chatbot works Three steps: Classify the message into an intent ( greeting , goodbye , python , training …). Pick one of that intent's responses. If the model isn't confident enough, say so (a fallback ). The whole bot is: training data → word counts → probabilities. 2. The training data: intents.json You teach Nova by writing examples, not code: { "tag" : "greeting" , "patterns" : [ "hello" , "hi" , "hey" , "good morning" , "good evening" , "how are you" , "hello chatbot" ], "responses" : [ "Hello! What would you like to learn?" , "Hi! Ask me about Python or AI." ] } patterns are example messages. responses are what Nova may answer. The starter file has 10 intents, 56 examples and 90 unique words. 3. Tokenization: text to words The model can't work with sentences directly, so we split them into lowercase words with one regular expression: TOKEN_RE = re . compile ( r " [a-z0-9 ' ]+ " ) def tokenize ( text : str ) -> list [ str ]: return TOKEN_RE . findall ( text . lower ()) >>> tokenize ( " Hi Nova! How ' s it going? " ) [ ' hi ' , ' nova ' , " how ' s " , ' it ' , ' going ' ] Punctuation disappears, capitals disappear, and apostrophes stay so "how's" remains one word. 4. Training is just counting "Training" Naive Bayes means counting three things for each intent: how many examples it has how often each word appears in them how many words it has in total for pattern in patterns : tokens = tokenize ( str ( pattern )) self . document_count += 1 self . intent_documents [ tag ] += 1 self . token_counts [ tag ]. update ( tokens ) self . total_tokens [ tag ] += len ( tokens ) self . vocabulary . update ( tokens ) For greeting in the starter data: 7 examples, 12 words in total, and "hello" appears 2 times. That's the whole trained model. It's saved as plain JSON, so you can open it and read it. 5. The math: Naive Bayes For a message, we want the intent with the highest probability given its words. Bayes' rule says that's proportional to: P(intent) × P(word₁ | intent) × P(word₂ | intent) × … The "naive" part is assuming the words are independent. It's not really true, but it works surprisingly well for short messages. The prior , how common the intent is: P(intent) = (examples in intent + 1) / (all examples + number of intents) The likelihood , how typical a word is for the intent: P(word | intent) = (count of word in intent + 1) / (words in intent + vocabulary size) Real numbers for "hello" in greeting : (2 + 1) / (12 + 90) = 3 / 102 ≈ 0.029 . Why the "+1"? (Laplace smoothing) Without it, a word the intent has never seen gets probability 0, and multiplying by 0 wipes out the whole score. One unknown word, like "Nova", would make every intent impossible. Adding 1 to every count gives unseen words a small chance instead of zero. Why logs? Multiplying many small probabilities gives numbers so tiny that a computer rounds them to zero. So we add logarithms instead of multiplying: score = math . log ( prior ) for token in tokens : likelihood = ( self . token_counts [ intent ][ token ] + 1 ) / denominator score += math . log ( likelihood ) 6. From scores to confidence: softmax The log scores aren't percentages. To turn them into probabilities that add up to 1, we use softmax, subtracting the highest score first so exp() never overflows: highest = max ( scores . values ()) exponentials = { name : math . exp ( score - highest ) for name , score in scores . items ()} normalizer = sum ( exponentials . values ()) probabilities = { name : value / normalizer for name , value in exponentials . items ()} The top probability is Nova's confidence . If it's below the threshold (0.25), Nova falls back instead of guessing. 7. The cold start problem (real results) With the starter data, here's what Nova actually does: "what is python" → python , 59.5% "hello" → greeting , 30.3% "Hi Nova!" → fallback (greeting was top at only 23.4% , under the 25% threshold) "What's the weather in Paris?" → fallback , 19.3%, which is correct, since Nova knows nothing about weather Why does "Hi Nova!" fail? "Nova" never appears in the training data, so it adds nothing useful, and "hi" is only one short example among 56. The fix is data, not code. I added four greeting patterns, "hi nova", "hey nova", "hello nova" and "hi there nova", and retrained: "Hi Nova!" → greeting , 79.5% Same algorithm, four more lines of JSON, from 23% to 79%. In the video, I keep improving the examples and Nova reaches 96% on it. That's the main lesson of the whole project: a small model with good examples beats a clever model with bad ones. 8. Serve it with FastAPI The API is three endpoints: health, chat and retrain. class ChatRequest ( BaseModel ): message : str = Field ( min_length = 1 , max_length = 1000 ) @app.post ( " /api/chat " , response_model = ChatResponse ) def chat ( request : ChatRequest ) -> ChatResponse : message = request . message . strip () if not message : raise HTTPException ( status_code = 422 , detail = " Message cannot be blank " ) with model_lock : reply , prediction = bot . reply ( message ) return ChatResponse ( reply = reply , intent = prediction . intent , confidence = round ( prediction . confidence , 4 )) Pydantic rejects empty or huge messages for free, and the lock keeps a retrain from swapping the model in the middle of a reply. A small HTML/JS page in web/ calls /api/chat and shows the answer with its intent and confidence. Run it yourself git clone https://github.com/rainyreaksmey/build-chatbot-from-scratch cd build-chatbot-from-scratch python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt python train.py uvicorn app:app --reload Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 to chat, or http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs for the interactive API. To teach Nova something new, add an intent to data/intents.json with several differently-worded patterns, then run python train.py again. Don't expose /api/train publicly without authentication. Recap An intent chatbot = classify the message, then pick a response. Training Naive Bayes is just counting words. Laplace smoothing (+1) keeps unknown words from zeroing everything out. Logs prevent tiny-number underflow, and softmax turns scores into a confidence. A fallback threshold is better than a confident wrong answer. Better examples fixed the bot, not more code. Full walkthrough with every line typed live: https://youtu.be/kdIUMAgwrcU What should Nova learn next? Tell me in the comments. Drafted with AI assistance. The code and numbers come from the recorded run. I make AI, coding and tech tutorials on RainyTech .

title: Why SEO Is Important for Small Businesses in 2026
author: shamil vaniyambhulavan
summary: Many small businesses have great products and services, but potential customers still struggle to find them online. Why does this happen? In many cases, the problem is not the quality of the business. It is the lack of online visibility. This is where Search Engine Optimization (SEO) becomes important. SEO helps businesses improve their visibility in search engines and connect with people who are already searching for their products or services. What Is SEO? Search Engine Optimization is the process of improving a website so that search engines can better understand its content and users can discover relevant pages through organic search results. SEO includes several important activities, such as keyword research, content optimization, technical SEO, website performance improvements, and link building. The goal is not simply to attract more visitors. It is to attract the right audience. 1. Keyword Research Helps You Understand Customers Before creating website content, businesses should understand what their potential customers are searching for. For example, a local business might target specific searches such as: Digital marketing services for small businesses Best digital marketer in Malappuram Website development services near me These phrases represent different customer needs. Understanding search intent helps businesses create pages that answer those needs. Tools such as Google Keyword Planner and Google Search Console can help identify keyword opportunities and understand website performance. 2. Local SEO Helps Nearby Customers Find You Local SEO is especially useful for businesses that serve a particular city, town, or region. A properly optimized Google Business Profile, consistent business information, genuine customer reviews, and useful location-specific website content can help improve local visibility. For example, a business serving Malappuram should clearly explain its services and service area on its website. However, local rankings are not guaranteed. They depend on several factors, including relevance, distance, and prominence. 3. Helpful Content Builds Trust Publishing blog posts is not just about adding keywords to a website. Good content answers real questions, solves problems, and helps readers make informed decisions. A small business website can publish articles about common customer problems, service comparisons, frequently asked questions, and practical solutions. Instead of repeating the same keyword throughout an article, focus on writing naturally and covering the topic thoroughly. 4. Technical SEO Makes Your Website Easier to Understand Even useful content can struggle if a website has technical problems. Some important technical SEO practices include: Making the website mobile-friendly. Improving page loading performance. Using clear page titles and meta descriptions. Fixing broken internal links. Creating a logical website structure. Checking indexing and crawling issues. Google Search Console is useful for identifying indexing problems and monitoring how pages perform in Google Search. 5. Quality Backlinks Can Support Website Authority Backlinks are links from other websites to your website. Relevant links can help people discover your content and provide context about your website. However, not every backlink is valuable. Focus on earning links through useful articles, industry contributions, professional profiles, genuine partnerships, and original resources. Avoid creating large numbers of low-quality links just to manipulate rankings. Quality and relevance matter more than the number of links alone. A Simple SEO Plan for Small Businesses If you are starting SEO for your business, follow these steps: Identify your target audience and the keywords they use. Optimize your main service pages. Set up and maintain your Google Business Profile if eligible. Publish useful, original blog content. Improve your website's mobile experience and technical health. Earn relevant backlinks naturally. Monitor impressions, clicks, rankings, and enquiries using Google Search Console and analytics tools. SEO is an ongoing process. Results can take time, and no single technique guarantees a first-page ranking. Final Thoughts Small businesses do not always need a large marketing budget to begin improving their online visibility. They need a clear strategy, useful content, a technically sound website, and consistent effort. When SEO focuses on solving customer problems rather than simply targeting search engines, it can become a valuable part of long-term business growth.
